speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: ANNUAL REPORT OF COMMISSIONER OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Commissioner of Official Languages submitted his annual report to us. To everyone's surprise and great disappointment, he does not mention the city of Sault Ste. Marie, which nevertheless attracted a lot of attention earlier this year, and which I have denounced publicly.
I would point out to him that since 1987, about fifty Ontario municipalities have openly proclaimed themselves unilingual English. This is horrible! However, he does not mention that in his report.
Although the Commissioner is not a prophet, he could certainly have felt, like many French Canadians, this great linguistic malaise that exists in Canada and is rampant in some towns and cities, but he did not even see fit to mention it in his preliminary remarks.
A city or town like Sault Ste. Marie which declares itself to be unilingual English needlessly humiliates its French minority. Groups like APEC, the Alliance for the Preservation of English in Canada, a reactionary association that feeds on the fears and prejudices of past centuries, now seem to be spreading across Canada. There is also the COR (Confederation of Regions) Party, which like all the others propagates racist, anti-French ideas that are dangerous for our democracy.
We will probably have to wait until next year, Mr. Speaker, to know the extent of this concern. All I hope is that it will not be too late.

4-H NATIONAL CITIZENSHIP SEMINAR

subtopic: ANNUAL REPORT OF COMMISSIONER OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week Ottawa is playing host to Canada's 4-H delegates during their National Citizenship Seminar.
These young people from across our country will be discussing Canadian government systems, their rights and responsibilities as citizens, and they will be learning about each other.
All members should be proud of these young adults who were selected as delegates for their outstanding achievements in their local and provincial 4-H activities. I am proud that several of these exceptional young Canadians are from Prince Edward Island.
Head, heart, hands and health is the 4-H motto. This great national organization provides young people with the opportunity to develop both leadership and life skills and, in doing so, contribute to the well-being of our communities.
On behalf of all members of the House, I commend these young people for their accomplishments to date and wish them every success in their future endeavours.

Mr. Speaker, very soon members of this House will be voting on the goods and services tax. Close to 80 per cent of Canadians oppose the tax, but the government has chosen not to listen.
Only 21 of the 167 Conservative MPs need to vote with the combined opposition parties to defeat the tax, so we are urging Canadians across the country to phone their Conservative members of Parliament and tell them to vote against the GST.
In Atlantic Canada, Canadians can phone the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants at 542-5737; the member for South Shore at 543-5141; the member for Halifax West at 865-9194; the member for Fredericton-York- Sunbury at 458-8046; the member for St. John's East at

739-0802; the member for Fundy-Royal at 433-4040; or the member for Carleton-Charlotte at 466-3670.

Mr. Speaker, this evening, the second Gala des Grands Quebecois will take place in Quebec City, organized by the Chambre de commerce et de lindustrie du Quebec metropolitan.
On behalf of my colleagues from the Quebec City region, I wish to pay tribute to three famous people who will receive the title of Grand Quebecois this evening: painter Jean-Paul Lemieux, businessman Jacques Moris-set and Senator Renaude Lapointe, who in their respective careers have always been an honour to Quebec City and the general area.
Mr. Speaker, they will join Senator Jean-Marie Poi-tras, author Roger Lemelin and Father Georges-Henri Levesque, who last year became the first members of the Academie des Grands Quebecois.
Speaking on behalf of the residents of the Quebec City region and especially those of Montmorency-Orleans, I want to thank these three laureates for their outstanding contribution to the economic, social, cultural life of our beautiful region.

Mr. Speaker, last week the government announced it had approved the agreement in principle for the largest comprehensive aboriginal claim in Canada. This is the claim of the 17,000 Inuit of the central and eastern Arctic.
The elements of this deal were arrived at by the negotiating parties last December. In February, the agreement in principle was approved by the Inuit negotiators. Last week's approval by the federal cabinet is another major step toward a final agreement.
The Inuit negotiators who persevered over the past 14 years of negotiations deserve our thanks and congratulations.
A formal signing ceremony is planned for late April or early May, in Igloolik, to which the Prime Minister has been invited. I urge the Prime Minister to accept this invitation.
I also encourage the government to keep the door open for the Dene and Metis in the western Arctic. Justice requires a continued commitment to the fair settlement of both the Inuit and the Dene-Metis claims.

Mr. Speaker, April 4 is Refugee Rights Day when Canadians from coast to coast celebrate the Supreme Court of Canada's decision five years ago today that every person in Canada who claims to be a refugee has the right to an oral hearing.
Ever since that day this government has tried to get around that decision, the UN Convention on Refugee Status and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It refused the quick and fair method for deciding refugee status asked for by Rabbi Plaut, all Canadian churches, Canadian labour, the parliamentary committee on labour, employment and immigration and every independent witness who testified on Bill C-55.
Instead, the government created a tangled, slow and unfair system that has built up a backlog of 21,000 claimants since January 1989 whose cases have not yet been decided.
Now, desperate because 1,900 of this year's claimants are waiting in Newfoundland for decisions, this government imposes still more transit visa restrictions on international travellers through Gander and Mirabel.
On behalf of all Canadians who help real refugees, I call on this government to stop stalling and enact the quick and fair system Canadians asked for.
April 4, 1990

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY FORUM ON GLOBAL CLIMATE CHANGE
PARLIAMENTARY FORUM ON GLOBAL CLIMATE CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Forum on Global Climate Change will begin here on Monday, April 23. This is a unique effort of eight standing committees of this House. For the first time committees have joined together to organize a group of expert witnesses who can give a rounded view on a problem of common interest. The forum will form part of a study of the environmental aspects of each committee's field of interest.
The eight organizing committees are delighted that you, Mr. Speaker, with your well-known interest in the environment, will be the opening speaker of the plenary session to begin at 10.30 on Monday, April 23.
As this forum progresses with joint meetings of the participating committees, which will each have chosen a major speaker, I believe parliamentarians and the public will become much better informed with a balanced view on climate change.
Our special proceedings will undoubtedly become excellent reference material on this topic.
I want to thank the many people on all sides of this House who have worked to make this Parliamentary Forum on Global Climate Change a reality.

Mr. Speaker, I have hundreds of letters here from my constituents urging the Government of Canada to demonstrate support for the Lithuanian people by recognizing the newly-elected government of the Republic of Lithuania. I will ask a page to deliver these to the Secretary of State for External Affairs directly.
Tonight, the Baltic Federation in Canada in conjunction with a committee of parliamentarians is holding its eighteenth annual Baltic evening. This event is a very special event as, historically, the Baltic peoples have held a very special place in the hearts of Canadians.
Tonight's Baltic evening, however, will be unprecedented in its historic significance since, among the guests, we will have the honour of hosting the first
democratically elected Vice-President of the Republic of Lithuania in fifty years, Professor Bronius Kuzmickas.
On behalf of all Canadians to whom democracy is fundamental and human rights are non-negotiable, I say to Mr. Kuzmickas whom I had the pleasure of meeting in Lithuania: Welcome to Canada. We are very proud to have you on Canadian soil.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the U.S. Senate witnessed an historic vote when the vast majority of its members passed a new clean air bill.
The bill concentrates on three specific areas: urban pollution, toxic emissions and acid rain. More specifically, I may say that an annual reduction of ten million tons in sulphur dioxide emissions meets the expectations of and is a response to pressure by the Canadian government on U.S. authorities. All Canadians have reason to rejoice, now that our U.S. neighbours have taken this giant step to protect the environment.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the major contribution made by Senator George Mitchell, who has always been Canada's staunchest ally in our fight against acid rain. The door is now wide open for negotiations on a bilateral agreement on acid rain, a plan dear to the heart of the Prime Minister of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, today I am sure all members of the House will want to join me in congratulating the United States Senate in passing the Clean Air Act last evening by a vote of 89 to 11.
Hear, hear!

I would like to commend Senator George Mitchell, the U.S. senate majority House leader, for guiding through the legislation and for fulfilling his

April 4, 1990
Oral Questions
commitment to get the bill passed. This bill will provide significant reductions in acid rain crossing into Canada.
I might say that I had the privilege of extending my congratulations by telephone this morning to Senator Mitchell.
We are now hoping that the Elouse of Representatives will introduce and pass this important legislation in order that it can become law this year and we can all breathe a little easier on both sides of the 49th parallel with cleaner air.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Yesterday after Question Period the Minister of the Environment said outside the House that Canada's energy ministers were being "too timid" about slashing carbon dioxide emissions. The environment minister went on to say: "We must be bolder".
Does the minister of energy agree with his colleague the Minister of the Environment? If so, will he today stop being timid and take bold steps to set targets to reduce air pollution in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, the hon. member talks about being too timid. If that accusation is valid for me, I imagine it is valid for some other people in this House, too.
I want to get directly to the question that the hon. member asked since it is a serious and important question.
After the Toronto conference energy ministers over the two-year period since 1988 looked clearly at what a 20 per cent reduction of CO2 emissions, plus all growth, either industrial or through the use of private motor fuels, would mean in terms of the ability of Canadians to meet the target presented at the Toronto conference for the years between 1988 and 2005.
The first point that has to be made is that that would be a reduction of between 44 per cent and 50 per cent. That is the base line from which we would have to start.
The task force that we commissioned as ministers of energy released a report publicly which states in part: "It is believed that achievement of a 20 per cent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions by 2005 could cause significant economic dislocation and would likely require significant changes in lifestyle."
Table it.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: It has been made public. I can send hon. members a copy any time they want one.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps we could proceed to the second question and the minister could continue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 10, 1989, over a year ago, the Prime Minister and 23 other heads of government signed the Declaration of The Hague which states:
Today, the very conditions of life on our planet are threatened by
severe attacks to which the earth's atmosphere is subjected.
If the Minister of the Environment said yesterday that energy ministers, including his own colleague, were being "too timid" about slashing carbon dioxide emissions and that "we must be bolder", what is he going to do to protect his own credibility to get his colleague to act in this matter? Or, does he disagree both with him and with his Prime Minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I never said the word "timid"; never, never in my life.
Oh, oh!
We all know that not one of my colleagues is timid. They are all bold and courageous.
Hear, hear!

At least they are not timid with me.
What I said is that I hope Canada will be at the forefront of the fight against pollution and CO2 emissions.
April 4, 1990

We will have a very good opportunity during the next month to test to what extent Canadians are willing to accept the radical changes that are needed to reach the targets we would like to set.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the journalists who reported his comments will be happy to release their transcripts of what they heard him say.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, according to the newspapers, the minister said that the statement by the Energy ministers had some positive aspects, including the need for continuing the fight against emissions, but, he said, we must do more. If that is his position, what specific recommendations does he have today for his government? And if he doesn't want to give us his recommendations, how can we take him seriously on a subject that is so important to the future of this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that this government will be the first in the history of Canada to set targets in terms of CO2 reduction.
The decisions we have to make will have to be taken by 1992, at least, when the other countries of the world, led for the most part by Canada, will enter into an international convention to deal with climate change. If it is possible, we should do it earlier. I say "if possible" because we are dealing with possibilities here.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the acting Prime Minister.
For months we on this side of the House have been telling the government that it is not doing enough to promote the Official Languages Act and that that failure is a direct cause of much of the language tension in this country.
More specifically, we have demanded that the regulations relating to the Official Languages Act, passed 21 months ago in this House, be tabled. Still we have no regulations and no action.
Oral Questions
This morning in an interview on radio station CHEZ-106 the Commissioner of Official Languages, D'Iberville Fortier, also criticized the government's slowness in acting. In fact the commissioner has threatened to resign in order to protest the absolute lack of action by this government.
Will the Prime Minister or the acting Prime Minister tell this House that he finally accepts the fact that the government has failed in this dossier and that it is a part of a major problem in this country that has to be addressed and resolved soon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are well aware of the situation with respect to official languages in this country. I had a chance to consult with the commissioner just a few days ago, before he released his report. We had a frank chat about it.
As I mentioned yesterday in answer to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, Bill C-72 imposes a rather complex and rather special process for consultation. This process has been gone through, after the first project of regulations was prepared. Obviously, if you are going to have consultations, the net presumption is that you are going to listen to the people you consult with.
Thus a second project was prepared. The next round of consultations will be getting under way veiy shortly with the major players, including the Commissioner of Official Languages.
This is very important. It is the first reform in 19 years. We want it to be meaningful. We want it to be well accepted, fair and equitable for all Canadians.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we phoned all the agencies today. Consultations have taken place and have now been completed, but I will get back to that later.
I would like to say to the minister that the Prime Minister of this country said the Commissioner of Official Languages was an impartial, sensitive and objective observer of language questions in this country. The Commissioner said on radio, yesterday or this morning, that it was as if the government were afraid to implement its own legislation which received practically unanimous support in the House two years ago. Considering these statements, does the minister responsible intend to table the regulations today or at least issue a statement

April 4, 1990
Oral Questions
with an action plan setting forth the Conservative Government's commitment to promoting official languages in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the action plan was already included in Bill C-72. The action plan is being implemented. The government's commitment is firm, and at the appropriate time, after full consultation with the parties concerned, we shall table the regulations in the House, in such a way that they are fair and equitable for all Canadians and are accepted by all linguistic communities in this country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. The Innu are once again before the courts. They are asking for an injunction to stop low-level flights.
The minister is aware that these flights are considered to be hazardous to the people of Labrador and to the environment. Will the minister finally demonstrate he is truly convinced that it is imporant to protect the environment and will he intervene to put a stop to these low-level flights?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will respond to that question. Obviously I cannot comment on a case that is before the courts.
As the hon. member knows, with respect to the proposed NATO flight training centre, we have indicated that no plans would proceed until there has been a full environmental review and that we would abide by the decisions of that review.
With respect to the existing low-level flights which are going on at Goose Bay, that comes about as a result of agreements which have been signed with our allies going back a number of years. We have agreed to introduce mitigative measures, to introduce monitoring to ensure that we avoid areas with wildlife or with people and to ensure that that activity is carried out in a very responsible manner.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of the Environment.
Will the minister co-operate with his colleagues, since environmental issues require joint action from different ministries? If the minister is serious about the environment then he should undertake to do this.
I want to raise another matter with the minister. In his discussion paper tabled last week there are several paragraphs on the Arctic.
We know from many other studies that have occurred before that the Arctic has been largely ignored and that, for example, two-thirds of the children on Broughton Island are suffering from unsafe levels of PCBs in their blood. We need action on the environment now, and we need action in the north.
For example, Inco has offered to assist the Soviet Union to reduce pollution. PCBs are a serious source of pollution in the Arctic. Since we have an international agreement with 17 countries, I am asking the minister if he will move now to discuss with these western countries changing the agreement on transferring technology to the Soviet Union so that we can deal with these serious Arctic problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party can see this consultation document is quite complete and sweeping in its scope. The Arctic has been dealt with in the consultation document.
The consultation process will allow us to put different options before Canadians concerning a comprehensive Arctic policy. As we know, the Prime Minister signed agreements with the Soviet Union during his last visit to that country, so we are heading in the right direction concerning the Arctic.
I admit we have much more to do. I hope we will have the support of Canadians to do it at the end of the consultation process.
April 4, 1990

Mr. Speaker, the minister will certainly have the support of Arctic Canadians, but there have been many recommendations on which he should act now.
I would raise an issue on CO2 emissions and the lack of action by this government. Yesterday, we saw the Senate in the United States at least taking some direct action on SO2 emissions, and in fact the member of Parliament for Parry Sound congratulating the Senate on doing that.
The minister knows full well that global warming will have extreme consequences in the Arctic. When will the minister take some leadership for Canada on the CO2 emissions and in setting those targets by 2005?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish the leader of the New Democratic Party would recognize the tremendous role that Canada has played in bringing the United States to this vote.
We all know that the acid rain issue was never raised in any meeting between the President of the United States and the former Prime Minister. Prime Minister Mulro-ney made it happen, and we should be proud of that as a country. As Canadians, this should be the day we enjoy it and be proud of it.
As far as CO2 emissions are concerned, we all know that Canada is at the forefront of countries fighting this pollution problem. We have made commitments on this. The consultation process will give Canadians the opportunity to tell us what they will be ready to pay for and what they will be ready to accept in terms of radical changes. I trust that it will be a joint enterprise.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. At a time when language tensions are escalating in this country, the government has done nothing to implement Bill C-72, which was passed by this House 20 months ago to promote bilingualism and to deal with such issues.
Oral Questions
In August, 1989 the President of the Treasury Board told this House that regulations relating to the Official Languages Act would be tabled before the end of last year. This morning, the media reported that the minister now has said that they would be tabled some time after June 23. When after June 23? What year?
I want to ask the Prime Minister or the Acting Prime Minister, will he give us a date when these regulations will be tabled and we can deal with these issues in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to answer my hon. colleague's allegation that I mentioned June 23 as any kind of a date relating to the regulations. Never, never.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: You said that and we have you on tape.

I would like to have a copy, because I never said that.
The regulations will be tabled in this House as soon as the process set out and agreed to by all members of the House who voted for Bill C-72 is fully completed. They are well on the way. We have worked assiduously to complete the regulations, to go through the consultation process, to revise the regulations as a result of the consultations and to finalize those consultations as of now.
As soon as those are finalized, we will be tabling the regulations in this House.

Mr. Speaker, if the government is doing such a great job, why is the Commissioner of Official Languages threatening to quit his job?
We have contacted the different language associations in this country, and they have stated that they have already consulted with the government.
The Commissioner of Official Languages said that 80 per cent of federal institutions are not applying the 1988 Official Languages Act. He said: "Who is to blame when you are listening to a symphony and it is poorly played? You can say that the conductor has an important role in this."
Once again I want to ask the minister when will he table the regulations? Can he give us an exact date when

April 4, 1990
Oral Questions
he will table these regulations, considering that the consultations have already taken place? What is holding him up? Who is he afraid of?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly not the opposition.
It is very simple, the regulations will be completed as soon as the process set out in Bill C-72 is fully completed.
It is already 20 months.

We have wasted no efforts to complete that process. That process is still on-going. We are following the law, which may be a strange concept to some people opposite. We are following Bill C-72 and we will table the regulations as soon as the process is completed.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Finance told Canadians that they were not legally required to repay old age pension funds and family allowance funds because the clawback scheme that the government has put forward has still not been passed by Parliament.
Subsequently, the Department of National Revenue has stated that it will calculate what would be due and withhold refunds.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance today who has it right? Are those people obliged to pay those amounts now or is the Department of National Revenue going to get its way and withhold the funds?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as with any budgetary provisions, obviously the taxpayer has the right to file a notice of objection at which time the payment would be assessed. When and if the provision becomes law and receives Royal Assent, then there has to be a re-assessment and the tax-back provision would come into effect.
The taxpayer has a choice. But as I stated yesterday, we urge Canadians to comply with the provisions that are stated in the Ways and Means motion in order to prevent the ensuing confusion that may take place at a later date. As of today and before Royal Assent is given, the taxpayer has the option to file a notice of objection or comply with the Ways and Means motion which is currently on the books.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. A number of people in Alberta, people generally, the premier, the treasurer of that province all oppose the goods and services tax because they are very much aware of what kind of havoc the GST will bring to Alberta. The Government of Alberta has produced a study showing that the impact on Albertans will be very, very serious.
Will the Minister of Finance admit to Albertans that, in fact, his goods and services tax is going to fuel inflation in that province as well as across the country, maintain high interest rates in Canada, and reduce consumer spending in Alberta and across the nation? Will he come clean with Albertans today?

Mr. Speaker, I have come clean with Albertans. I have said precisely what our analysis shows the impact will be in the province of Alberta. Alberta will benefit from the replacement of the manufacturers' sales tax with the goods and services tax to a greater extent than any other province in the country: close to 3 per cent in terms of increased income.
I have made the point, as my hon. friend has heard me say, that Albertans today are paying $685 for every man, woman and child through the manufacturers' sales tax. That has hardly changed as a result of the replacement of that tax with the goods and services tax.
It is very hard to understand the impact that the Alberta government says the GST will have on consumer spending. Where the impact will be felt will be because of the fact that Albertans are major exporters and that is where the GST will benefit their economy. Albertans will benefit because the cost of capital or the cost of a new oil well or a new pulp and paper plant will drop in price and also because the Alberta economy will benefit from opportunities to expand and diversify as a result of the combination of the federal sales tax being replaced by the goods and services tax and the free trade agreement.
April 4, 1990

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Health. It has been revealed this week that the Department of Health has secretly commissioned further studies into the Meme breast implant. Yet the official position of the department remains that of the Kerrigan report that women should not worry.
Given that the government-commissioned Kerrigan report has been widely discredited, even called a plagiary by one leading researcher in the field, will the minister finally admit that his department has been misleading Canadian women on the safety of this implant, and will he withdraw this dangerous product from the marketplace until it is proven safe?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would take more time than I have to correct all the inaccuracies in the hon. member's question. Let me, however, indicate a number of things to him.
First, we have not commissioned secret reports. A number of researchers have come to us to make proposals for research that they would like to do, which we have agreed to finance, and I think it is appropriate that we should do that. We have not had concerns which led us to commission reports.
Second, one of the reports that the member claims to be commissioned, which is being done by the Ottawa Heart Institute, is looking at all aspects of polyurethane in implants in Canada. It is not simply looking at the Meme breast implant.
Third, there have been some 12,000 Meme breast implants sold in Canada since 1984. The incidence of failure among the Meme is considerably lower than the failure rate among other breast implants. That should be a matter of which the hon. gentleman should be aware.
Additionally, there is a good deal of question about research that was alleged to have discredited the Meme when the hon. member gave his press conference earlier in the week.
I would like to make a proposal to the hon. member. Instead of going out and making false allegations, if the hon. member would like to have the facts, I would be
Oral Questions
pleased to have arranged for him a full briefing by officials within the department to give him the appropriate information so that he would have the information before making his allegations, instead of making his allegations first and seeking information after.

Mr. Speaker, both studies in the United States and in Canada show that this implant deteriorates within the body and produces carcinogenic products which then are distributed throughout the woman's body. There is no necessity to keep this product on the market while it is being investigated, none whatsoever.
Remembering that there are 60 cases in the United States and more than one in Canada in which this issue is being raised because of the safety of the product, what is more important to the minister: the profits of a distributor and a handful of plastic surgeons, or the safety and health of Canadian women?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the approach that is being taken by the hon. member is irresponsible. What he does is to frighten women and he does so in a way that is totally irresponsible because he has not taken the effort to get the information before making these allegations.
The House will recall that a minute ago I simply offered to the hon. member to give him a full briefing in this matter. He did not indicate his willingness to take up the briefing. I would indicate to him as well that the University of Florida study to which he refers has been largely discredited. He would have known that if he had bothered to check his facts first.
I would like to repeat that invitation to him. I will make the invitation as well to our colleague from Winnipeg North who, unlike the hon. gentleman, has been responsible in seeking information first before making false allegations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. In light of the legislation passed last night in the United States Senate by a majority of 89 to 11,1 am sure the minister is gratified and I would hope that his ministry will now be pursuing in every way with his provincial counterparts to ensure that we are doing

April 4, 1990
Oral Questions
everything within our power to control acid rain as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is right and we all know his interest on this great issue for Canada.
As a matter of fact, this vote moves us much closer to the opening of formal negotiations with the Americans. During last year, on many occasions, U.S. and Canadian officials have met to set up the framework and the essential elements of what the agreement could contain.
We think that those formal negotiations should begin very soon. We hope that it will be possible to conclude an agreement by the fall.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Health. I am a woman and I am very concerned about the Meme breast implant.
Why is the Minister of Health placing at risk all women in this country? The American manufacturer of this product has stated that household polyfoam is not designed for implantation within the human body.
Why is the minister not removing this product from the market? Why is he placing the women of this country at great risk?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member says that I am threatening the health of all the women in this country. That sort of an exaggeration does no credit to the hon. member.
Why don't you turn your collar around?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If the hon. member will pay attention-
Get back on your tricycle.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
-the goal of all hon. members in the House, irrespective of which side of the House they sit on, should be to ensure the safety of all Canadians and not falsely create fear among Canadians. As a consequence, I would invite the hon. member to have a full
briefing with regard to this, to receive the information first before making false allegations of this nature.
For example, if the hon. member is referring to the University of Florida study, which was referred to by another hon. member earlier, any plastic subjected to very high temperatures, which do not exist in the human body, will break down into carcinogens. Mr. Speaker, I gave you notice of a question of privilege which I believe affects myself and other members of this House. In introducing the question of privilege, I would like to quote form the ruling you made in the House on April 14, 1987, a ruling that you referred to again on March 26, 1990. You said:
It is essential to our democratic system. The controversial issue should be debated at reasonable length so that every reasonable opportunity shall be available to hear the arguments pro and con and the reasonable delaying tactics should be permissible to enable opponents of a measure to enlist public support for their point of view. Sooner or later every issue must be decided and the decision will be taken by a majority. Rules of procedure protect both the minority and the majority. They are designed to allow the full expression of views on both sides of an issue. They provide the Opposition with a means to delay a decision. They also provide the majority with a means of limiting debate in order to arrive at a decision. This is the kind of balance essential to the procedure of a democratic assembly. Our rules were certainly never designed to permit the total frustration of one side or the other, the total stagnation of debate, or the total paralysis of the system.

time, at each and every stage of the bill? That is significant to the privileges of each member of the House and it is significant to the privileges of all members of this House.

**********I

people to a certain extent. Mr. Kindy, Mr. Kilgour, people like that, are expelled.

Mr. Speaker, I think what the Canadian people should be realizing today is that what we are seeing from the Conservative government across the way is some of the heaviest handed tactics we have seen in the history of this parliamentary democracy. What we are seeing are jack-

boot tactics by the Conservative party across the way to impose a tax that over 80 per cent of the Canadian people do not want.

I believe, as all of us do, that the only way we can advance debate is by coming up with alternatives.
For months a group of us worked together with tax experts from across the country. We even consulted Senators Bradley and Gephardt in the United States, Hall-Rabushka from the Hoover Institute at Stanford, Lyman Maclnnis, past president of the Ontario Institute of Chartered Accountants, and Thomas Hodgson, President of Central Guaranty Trust in Toronto, the whiz kid of Bay Street. We got together with the researchers at the Library of Parliament and with Statistics Canada which develops modelling systems, some of those same

Time Allocation
modelling systems that the Minister of Finance uses in his department.
We came up with a constructive alternative to the goods and services tax. We came up with an alternative that was fairer, simpler, efficient and workable. It was a system where we knew we had to obviate the need for a goods and services tax because of the amount of revenue it was going to bring in. We admitted that the manufacturers' sales tax, the federal sales tax, was not a good thing and in our program we phased it out over three years, not all at once. We knew we had to be revenue neutral. We came up with numbers that would allow us to meet all of those objectives.
We came up with a form, and we called it the single tax, and it is 25 per cent for individuals and 25 per cent for corporations. We gave very progressive, refundable tax credits to those people in our community who are disadvantaged. We admitted all the way through this that we were advancing debate.
We did not say that our ideas were conclusive. We sent our material to the Minister of Finance on several occasions, and asked him to refute it, to give it to his officials to criticize it and try to improve on it. Not once did I hear from his department, or from the minister. I have been listening for months to him saying there are absolutely no alternatives on this side of the House. Finally, when I got his ear today, he snuffed off 179 pages of hard work by men and women from academia, from business, and work done by chartered accountants. He said: "Oh, that is some little booklet, on a single tax that does not work".
He is blind and deaf to reality.

Well, I think the Minister of Finance is really losing it. He refuses to acknowledge that 80 per cent of people in this country are concerned about the goods and services tax. It is a tremendous disincentive to small business. It is causing fear for senior citizens.
Instead of listening and asking his departmental officials to do an analysis of that and point out the weaknesses, he continues to say there are absolutely no alternatives. I think the Minister of Finance is doing a tremendous disservice to his office.
It is only one alternative. I have said in this House before that this is not the Liberal Party position. We, in this party, right now, are going through a leadership debate. So we have three, four or five alternatives. But that is not the point.
Your leader is going to decide for you.

In fairness, we are a team. But that is no excuse for the Minister of Finance to ignore the idea. Whether this idea came from a member of the New Democratic Party or whether this idea came from a Conservative member, or whether it came from industry, it does not matter. It is the responsibility of the Minister of Finance to look at a constructive alternative to a tax that is just crippling the spirit of this country.
We have said in this House before and many Liberal members have said that the current tax system is not just the product of members opposite, it is the product of many governments over many years. The point is that right now it is 15,000 pages of rules and exceptions to exceptions. Even the best accountants and tax lawyers in this country will readily admit today that they no longer understand it. It is out of control. Canadians are being so frustrated by the current Income Thx Act that it is time for this government to take the lead and clean it up.
The government always talks about productivity. We lack productivity because, generally speaking, Canadians do not feel there is fairness in the tax system. A man who is working on a shop floor making $20 an hour might pay $8 a week in tax on that hourly wage and at the end of the year he might pay another $1,500 or $2,000. His neighbour next door might be an architect or a tax lawyer who is making $150,000 a year and he will not be paying any tax. We know that is not right.
The tax system, with all its legal tax preferences, is so imbalanced right now, that the person who is working his heart and guts out on the shop floor says: "Why should I work so hard when my neighbour who is making three times as much does not pay anything?". That system does not work.
If we are going to have fairness and productivity and if we are going to get a nation that can be a world-class competitor again, we must start with the tax system. A goods and service tax that adds another 45 or 50 pages to the 45 or 50 pages that every individual in Canada receives right now, is not the way to go.

One of the members said today that he phoned his constituents and indicated that he had enough constituents who were supportive of the goods and services tax.
I can tell you that in my riding it is the exact opposite. It is not that the people do not want to pay tax. People just want something that is fair, simple and efficient. The current system does not provide that.
This is one idea. Professor Brooks has another idea. I think it is the responsibility of this government to do a full analysis of this. We are already at the third draft in our proposal. It is the government's responsibility to respond.
The disincentive factor that is caused by this goods and services tax is going to force a further underground economy. Right now they guestimate that there is $40 billion to $50 billion in an underground economy in this country. If we had a system that was more fair we could probably recapture some of that underground economy. There might be enough to develop a national day care program.
But this government is so obsessed with cutting and retreating from programs that it is forgetting that there is a creative process. Instead of trying to develop ways to make the pie larger and renewing the spirit of productivity, it is cutting. This government has been retreating from national responsibility for the last six years. If it keeps going like this, it will be history within the next two years.

Mr. Speaker, I have been travelling with the finance committee on the GST debate. It has been almost three years since the finance minister informed Canadians through the tax reform White Paper how he planned to replace the 65 year-old manufacturers' sales tax.
The bill has already met with the expected enthusiastic response from the opposition parties in the House of Commons. But the many benefits for the whole economy of a broadly based goods and services tax far outweighs the criticism to date of this government proposal.
There is a major problem with the manufacturers' sales tax. The MST is applied to business inputs. That is the materials, parts and supplies used in the manufacturing process. This makes it tougher for Canadian export-
Time Allocation
ers to sell their products in foreign markets and compete with producers who pay no tax on their business inputs. In other words, being uncompetitive costs Canada jobs.
Surely it is time for us to take an honest look at the manufacturers' sales tax, that 13.5 per cent bite on most things made in Canada that has been conveniently hidden for too long. Suppose this tax did not exist and suppose your provincial premier, myself being from Ontario, Premier Peterson, decided to impose a similar provincial tax on manufacturers, there would be a great public outcry. There would be a charge that Ontario jobs would be lost and that business could not stand the competition from other tax-free provinces.
Or, suppose that the city of Cambridge or the city of Kitchener decided to impose its own manufacturers' sales tax on industry within those city limits? The move would be denounced as driving businesses to other communities such as Guelph, Brantford and Woodstock.
What are some of the concerns with the manufacturers' sales tax? First, it applies to a very narrow base. There are five commodities; tobacco, alcohol, automobiles, automobile parts and motor fuels. They represent about 16 per cent of government spending and yet they generate about one-third of the revenue from the manufacturers' sales tax. People who come here always ask why gas is so much cheaper south of the border. Why is tobacco so much cheaper? Why is alcohol so much cheaper? It is those five products that pay a heavy burden with the manufacturers' sales tax.
Another thing that Canadians have heard is that over the past 60 years there has been fiddling with the tax to satisfy one special interest group over another. As a result, there has been some 22,000 special provisions; including things such as athletic headbands. An athletic headband is considered clothing. Therefore, it is exempt from the manufacturers' sales tax. But if you buy an athletic wristband, it is considered sporting equipment and therefore is taxed.
A facial tissue is considered a cosmetic product and the MST is included in the price. The makers of facial tissues will argue that it is a health care product and, as such, should be exempt from the MST. If the makers are successful in winning that argument then they do not

April 4, 1990
Time Allocation
have to pay the tax. The tax they do not pay eventually is picked up by consumers somewhere else.
Another concern about the existing manufacturers' sales tax, the tax we want to get rid of, is the impact it has on domestically produced commodities. For example, I was talking about cosmetics. There are various rates. The reason for various rates depends on how a company handles its marketing and distribution function. On some cosmetics on the shelf the effective federal tax is as low as 5.8 per cent. On other products it is as high as 19.2 per cent.
Here we have similar products made by different companies in the same industry and yet we have a wide range of tax. I could not take you into a store and point out which product has the 6 per cent MST and which one has a 19 per cent effective rate. That is the type of situation with which we are dealing.
Small appliances have rates as low as 5.5 per cent and some as high as 13.9 per cent. Here we have within Canada again, companies competing against themselves but charged different rates of tax. They are trying, through the courts, to lessen their tax burden. They do so by setting up new corporate structures so they can change market distribution and reduce tax.
Another major concern is the impact on imported goods and exports. For example, office machines and equipment. For a domestic producer the MST rate is as low as 12 per cent to as high as 13 per cent. The important fact is that for a foreign company, the effective rate to that company on MST when it imports office machines and equipment is 7.5 per cent. Right away the Canadian domestic producer of office machines and equipment is at a 5 per cent disadvantage. He is at a 5 per cent disadvantage because of a tax his own country is charging. Canada is the only country that has a manufacturers' sales tax of this type, and when we consider that 40 per cent of our income comes from exports it is ludicrous that we maintain this tax.
I can think of one benefit of the manufacturers' sales tax, which has really been for politicians only. That is the fact that it is virtually invisible to consumers. Some people say "what you don't know won't hurt you".
Many people did not know that they were already paying a federal sales tax. A one-income family with two children and an income of $35,000 today is paying a manufacturers' sales tax on the average consumer basket of about $1,500. After the introduction of the GST they will pay about the same amount. For this particular family there is no change.
We have gone from a tax you can see to a tax you cannot see. I think the people of this country have reacted because they are suddenly seeing something which has been there for many years. Almost since its introduction, the MST has been a problem to manufacturers. We have heard of the many royal commissions that addressed its fundamental flaws in 1940, 1966 and 1983. Each study has recommended major change.
Canada is the only industrialized country with a manufacturers' sales tax of this kind. In 1990, the manufacturers' sales tax fails every test of good tax policy. At the age of 65 it is time to retire the manufacturers' sales tax.
No one should suggest that the GST is 100 per cent perfect. But when you compare it to the existing manufacturers' sales tax, the GST is a clear winner, a gold medal winner.
Tell that to your voters.

I will tell it to the voters.
According to the C.D. Howe Institute, the adoption of the GST would be the single most significant, recent advance in Canadian tax policy. The study states that the GST, by broadening the base of the tax to include currently untaxed goods and services, by changing the method of collection, will improve the efficiency of the Canadian economy.
So we have the C.D. Howe Institute, the Economic Council of Canada, the Conference Board of Canada who all support the improvement and the competitive position of Canadian manufacturing which they acknowledge will benefit the whole economy. They do not have any problem with the recommendation in Finance that it will create 60,000 new jobs every year.
The GST is a solution to a problem that most Canadians are unaware they have. There will not be any more royal commissions, any more study. This government has taken the daring and necessary step to reform the sales

We are clearly together, and I have been supporting this right from the beginning. We would like to improve it.
Naturally, we would like to have had a national sales tax that would have incorporated the federal and provincial sales tax systems, but this was not possible, given the political dynamics of the day. The issue is not those failed negotiations. The issue is the pressing need to proceed with reforming the tax system which is hurting Canadian business, and we are doing it in such a way that it leaves open the possibility of a truly national sales tax at a later date.
In conclusion, I would like to quote Terence Corcoran of The Globe and Mail. He said on December 8: "Think of the GST as a home renovation. It will make a bit of a mess while the work is being done, but the final result will be something you can be proud of".

Mr. Speaker, after having heard three members from the government side, I think it is inevitable that I, and my party, should share the same contempt for this government that the Canadian people feel as a result of the utter contempt this government has directed toward the Canadian people.
I listened to the member for Edmonton Northwest bleating about the efforts of the New Democratic Party representative on the finance committee. Whatever may be said about the efforts of my colleagues on that committee, they had one single purpose, and that was to ensure that all of the Canadian people were heard on this tax. We can understand why we heard the parliamentary secretary say: "We did not want to hear any more because they are all going to say the same thing." Eighty per cent of the Canadian people are going to say the same thing, that this tax is an unacceptable tax. It is a tax that must be opposed, and will be opposed.

We have heard my colleague talk of certain members on the government side who did not adhere to caucus discipline. I think it is important to know the fundamental elements that constitute the basis for that caucus discipline. I think it was best expressed by the hon. member for Simcoe Centre. She expressed it in ordinary language that everybody could understand: "If I listen to my constituents, I would not have time to give leadership."
We just heard the hon. member down the way say: "We are through with hearings. We are through with royal commissions. We are through with all that stuff. We made a decision." It is a decision which I said before is utterly contemptuous of the Canadian people.
Because the Canadian people have been denied the right to be heard adequately, the Ontario caucus of the New Democratic Party has for the last several days been holding hearings so at least Ontarians could be heard.
I think it is important, even before addressing the tax, to give you an impression of how Canadians are feeling. They feel that what is happening to their country as a result of the consistent actions of this government, tears at the very fabric of Canadian civilization, our humanitarian instincts and our sense of community. There is the sense that somehow our country is being robbed of so much that gave us pride and confidence, that in spite of everything, we could influence our fate and the destiny of this country.
But with the changes as a result of the free trade agreement, the cuts in UIC, privatization, deregulation, and other actions which have been opposed by the people but implemented by the government, it has created a terrible sense of powerlessness, frustration, anger and alienation. If the government wants to know why there seems to be so much division in this country then it should look for the answer in what it has done.
By creating a level playing field with the United States it has done what we predicted would happen. The Conservatives have made this country more like the United States. There are too many people out there who, frustrated with the government, are looking around for scapegoats. That is why we find so many of us looking for others to blame and exhibiting all kinds of character-

istics that are alien to our culture before this government came to power.
It is interesting that the Minister of Finance and the other member who talked about this bill to introduce the goods and services tax, did not at all attempt to defend the goods and services tax itself. They said only that the manufacturers' sales tax should be eliminated, that it cost jobs and that it should be eliminated in the interest of the growth of the Canadian economy.
We have never questioned that. The manufacturers' sales tax should be eliminated. But should it be replaced with a goods and services tax?
No.

Let us for a moment, Mr. Speaker, consider what the manufacturers' sales tax entailed. The manufacturers' sales tax led to $18.5 billion in revenue, whereas the goods and services tax will raise $21.5 billion in revenue. What is very interesting, if you look at the actual net gain in revenue, apart from the cost of administering the tax and rebates associated with the tax, all we would need to do is raise $14.5 billion. We can raise that $14.5 billion without having a goods and services tax, or the 4,000 people needed to collect that tax, simply by making small changes in a variety of taxes with no change in the establishment of the Department of National Revenue.
Let me list the changes. You can search for the details in the publication of Neil Brooks which was cited earlier.
Let us suppose we eliminate the MST and the GST but maintain the excise taxes on cigarettes and liquor. That is good for $2.3 billion. Eliminate the entertainment deductions for rich business people and the corporations; $1 billion. Tighten capital gains; $.5 billion. Eliminate all necessary tax breaks for corporations; $2 billion. Impose a minimum tax on corporations, the same as the Americans do; $2 million. Tax wealth either in the form of an inheritance or an annual tax on net wealth; $2.5 billion. Stop tax cheating as we used to before this government came to power; $3 billion. Restore the income tax to five rather than three marginal rates and raise the top marginal rate to 40 per cent. It is awfully interesting what the result of that is. Even the Minister
of Finance admits that inflation will increase by 1.25 per cent or more probably 3 per cent as a result of the GST.
The alternative would not only allow a fairer tax system and eliminate the problems of the MST, in fact it would cut inflation by 2.3 per cent. This, in turn, would mean that interest rates could be cut. If interest rates were cut investment would increase. If investment increased, jobs would be produced.
Yes, there is an alternative that is in the interests of the vast majority of Canadians. The Tories are not interested in the Canadian people, they show utter contempt and the people will show their utter contempt for a government that cares not for them or the country.

Mr. Speaker, it seems that we have near unanimity, at least on this side of the House and among those on the other side who refuse to be muzzled by their Whip that there is, on the part of the government, total and utter contempt for the wishes and needs of Canadians, total and utter contempt for the activities in this House.
A few moments ago we heard the Minister of Finance sneer contemptuously at the fact that we in the Liberal party did not have an alternative, and his associate minister held for his consideration a proposal by one of our colleagues, the member for Broadview-Greenwood, the single tax. What did they do? They say there are no alternatives. The Conservatives refuse to listen. They refuse to hear what Canadians have to say. They refuse to hear what Parliament has to say.
My colleagues from Alberta will know and appreciate these statistics. Since Standing Order 57, which refers to the closure motion, was adopted in 1913, it has been applied in this House 21 times to cut off debate from 1913 to December of 1988. In this Parliament, since 1988 that closure motion has been invoked 13 times.
Today we saw this motion applied in order to muzzle the backbenchers of the Conservative Party itself. How can Canadians get across their vehement dislike for this goods and services tax when the governing party has to put a muzzle on its own members?
I know all members on this side of the House think it is a shame that Canadians cannot debate the biggest tax fraud ever perpetrated against Canadians since Confederation. Mr. Speaker, I know you are going to give me 10 minutes to address this issue. We have seen the first application of a 7 per cent tax. I am only going to be able
